text: Socrates founds his city on need, and no prior idea of justice shapes its first form (Republic II, 369b–c). No one is self-sufficient, so the first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each doing the one work his nature suits (370a–c). A city that stayed at that size would never need a soldier. Glaucon refuses to live there and calls it a "city of pigs" (372d). He wants couches and side dishes, and Socrates grants him a city "with a fever" (372e). The growth of appetite in that city ends in war. The land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one, so the city must take a slice of its neighbors' land and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors follows of necessity, and with it comes the question that occupies the rest of the reading: what kind of person can be trusted with weapons? Socrates finds his model in a well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–e). From the dog he draws the first of the city's many surprises. The dog judges friend and enemy "by nothing other than knowing and not knowing" (376b), and the guardian tells friend from enemy the same way. Because his gentleness and fierceness follow knowledge, the guardian is already a philosopher of a kind.
